questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use circle properties to find angles or lengths and justify geometric conclusions.
questions.prompt: At point A on a circle, the tangent ray AX makes an acute angle of 34° with chord AB. A point C lies on the major arc AB. Find angle ACB and the smaller angle between OA and AB, where O is the centre.
questions.answer: Angle ACB is 34° and angle OAB is 56°.
questions.explanation: The tangent–chord theorem gives the angle subtended by AB at C. Radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent, so the acute tangent–chord angle and angle OAB add to 90°.

markingGuide.description: Applies the tangent–chord theorem to obtain 34°.
Uses the perpendicular radius and obtains 56°.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use circle properties to find angles or lengths and justify geometric conclusions.
questions.prompt: Two parallel chords of a circle lie on opposite sides of its centre. The radius is 13 cm and the chords are 10 cm and 24 cm long. Find the perpendicular distance between the chords.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre bisects each chord. The distances from the centre are sqrt(13² − 5²) = 12 cm and sqrt(13² − 12²) = 5 cm. Add them because the chords lie on opposite sides.

markingGuide.description: Halves the two chord lengths using the perpendicular-bisector property.
Finds both perpendicular distances as 12 cm and 5 cm.
Adds the distances and states 17 cm.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use circle properties to find angles or lengths and justify geometric conclusions.
questions.prompt: Two straight footpaths are tangent to a circular garden at A and B and meet outside it at P. The angle APB is 58°. Find the smaller angle AOB at the centre O.
questions.explanation: The radii to the contact points make angles of 90° with the paths. The sum of the interior angles of quadrilateral OAPB gives 360° − 90° − 90° − 58°.

markingGuide.description: Uses the perpendicularity of both radii to their tangents.
Subtracts the other three angles from 360° to obtain 122°.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use circle properties to find angles or lengths and justify geometric conclusions.
questions.prompt: A learner claims that an angle of 90° at C, subtended by a chord AB of a circle, could be formed even when AB misses the centre. Assess the claim and give a reason that applies to every possible position of C on the circle distinct from A and B.
questions.answer: The claim is false. AB must be a diameter.
questions.explanation: The arc AB opposite C has measure twice angle ACB, hence 180°. Its endpoints are opposite each other and the chord joining them passes through the centre.

markingGuide.description: Identifies that the intercepted arc measures twice the angle at C.
Obtains 180° for the intercepted arc.
Concludes that AB joins opposite points and passes through the centre.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use coordinates, gradients and midpoints to analyse geometric relationships.
questions.prompt: A survey plot has opposite corners A(−3, 7) and C(9, 1) of a parallelogram. A third corner is B(5, 9). Find the fourth corner D, assuming A, B, C and D occur in that order.
questions.explanation: Diagonals AC and BD have a common midpoint (3, 4). Reflect B through that midpoint to get D = (2 × 3 − 5, 2 × 4 − 9).

markingGuide.description: Finds the midpoint (3, 4) of AC.
Uses the bisection of BD to set up the unknown coordinates.
Obtains D(1, −1).

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use coordinates, gradients and midpoints to analyse geometric relationships.
questions.prompt: A line on a grid passes through (1, 7) and (7, 3). A second line through (4, 0) is perpendicular to it. Find the equation of the second line and use it to decide whether (8, 6) lies on that line.
questions.answer: The line is y = (3/2)(x − 4), and (8, 6) lies on it.
questions.explanation: The first gradient is −2/3, so its perpendicular has gradient 3/2. At x = 8, the second equation gives y = 6.

markingGuide.description: Finds the first gradient, −2/3.
Obtains perpendicular gradient 3/2 and the equation through (4, 0).
Substitutes x = 8 and confirms the point.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use coordinates, gradients and midpoints to analyse geometric relationships.
questions.prompt: A surveyor has A(2, −1), B(8, 2) and C(t, 6). Find the value of t for which C lies on the line through A and B. Using coordinates, show whether B is closer to A or C for this value of t.
questions.answer: t = 16, and B is closer to A.
questions.explanation: The rise from A to B is 3 over a run of 6, so the rise of 7 from A to C requires a run of 14. The squared distances from B to A and B to C are 45 and 80 respectively.

markingGuide.description: Finds and applies the common gradient to obtain t = 16.
Finds both squared distances, 45 and 80.
Compares the squared distances to conclude that B is closer to A.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Use coordinates, gradients and midpoints to analyse geometric relationships.
questions.prompt: A map shows a triangular market site with vertices A(−2, 1), B(6, 1) and C(4, 7). A boundary from C meets AB at D and divides the site so that triangle ACD has three times the area of triangle BCD. Find D.
questions.explanation: The triangles share the same height above AB. Their areas have ratio AD to DB. With AB = 8, AD = 3/4 × 8 = 6 and D is six units to the right of A.

markingGuide.description: Recognises the common altitude.
Uses AD:DB = 3:1 to obtain AD = 6.
Locates D at (4, 1).

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Represent finite sample spaces and calculate probabilities for single or successive events.
questions.prompt: Three fair coins are tossed together. List the outcomes containing exactly two heads, and find the probability that the middle coin is a tail given that exactly two heads occurred.
questions.answer: HHT, HTH and THH. The requested probability is 1/3.
questions.explanation: The three ordered outcomes are equally likely. Only HTH has a tail in the middle.

markingGuide.description: Lists all three admissible ordered outcomes.
Identifies HTH and obtains 1/3.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Represent finite sample spaces and calculate probabilities for single or successive events.
questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Determine whether the event that their sum is 7 and the event that the first die is even are independent. Justify your answer using probabilities.
questions.explanation: There are 6 outcomes with sum 7, and 18 outcomes with an even first die. Of the six sum-7 outcomes, three have even first values, namely (2, 5), (4, 3) and (6, 1). Thus 3/36 = (6/36) × (18/36).

markingGuide.description: Counts the 6 and 18 outcomes for the two events.
Counts the three joint outcomes.
Compares the joint probability with the product of the individual probabilities to conclude independence.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Represent finite sample spaces and calculate probabilities for single or successive events.
questions.prompt: A box contains five green counters and three yellow counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. A student calculates the probability of drawing at least one yellow as 3/8 + 3/8. Explain why this gives the wrong result and calculate the correct probability.
questions.answer: The correct probability is 9/14. Adding the two marginal probabilities counts the outcome of two yellow counters twice.
questions.explanation: Find the complement, two green counters. Its probability is (5/8) × (4/7) = 5/14. Subtract from one to get the required probability.

markingGuide.description: Explains the overlap in the two marginal events.
Computes the probability of two green counters as 5/14.
Uses the complement to obtain 9/14.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Represent finite sample spaces and calculate probabilities for single or successive events.
questions.prompt: A stall offers two ways to win. In game A, a fair die is rolled and the player wins if the result divides 6 exactly. In game B, two fair coins are tossed and the player wins if their faces match. Which game gives the greater chance of winning, and by how much?
questions.explanation: The winning die faces are 1, 2, 3 and 6, giving 4/6. Matching coin faces are HH and TT, giving 2/4. The difference is 4/6 − 2/4 = 1/6.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the four factors of six and finds the first probability.
Finds the second probability using HH and TT.
Compares the probabilities and states the difference as 1/6.
